MEMORANDUM FOR RECORD

SUBJECT: LD 2157, An Act to Prohibit the Unauthorized Use of Drones on or over the Premises of
Correctional Facilities and Jails

Committee Chair Senator Beebe-Center, Committee Chair Representative Hasenfus and my fellow
members of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety,
Thank you for allowing me to bring forth my bill, An Act to Prohibit the Unauthorized Use of Drones
on or over the Premises of Correctional Facilities and Jails.
Drones have become a popular and ubiquitous tool in our society and, like almost any tool, they can be used for both benign and nefarious purposes. One of those nefarious purposes is to deliver contraband to inmates into correctional facilities. Another is to perform surveillance and reconnaissance on correctional facilities to probe for weak spots in the security infrastructure.
A report by ABC News, just this last December, highlighted the fact that the use of drones in
smuggling drugs, cellphones and weapons into correctional facilities has sky-rocketed and become `a daily occurrence' . It also highlighted the fact that there are almost no cost-effective countenneasures
for bringing down a drone over a correctional facility. And while there was just 1 report of drones
being used in federal prisons to deliver contraband in 2015, there were 23 such reports in 2018, 5 7 in
2019, and 479 in 2024. The State of Georgia alone is now reporting that they had 70 such incidents just
in one month last year. Even here in Maine, DOC has reported the use of drones over the Long Creek
facility.

To make matters worse, drones are getting cheaper and the technology is getting better. They have better command and control systems, including pre-programmed flight software, they are lighter, have longer flight durations and can carry more weight. There are drones available now that can easily carry between 50 and 225 pounds. And their use
in criminal activity has risen in proportion with their capabilities.
Currently, while there are restrictions for operating drones (and other aircraft) over certain federal prisons that are part of a designated Air Defense Identification Zones
(ADIZ) under l4 CFR Part 99,and there are Temporary Flight Restrictions on a limited number of certain `high risk' federal prisons (see DOJ OIG Audit 20-104), there is no general prohibition for operating a drone over a correctional facility under 14 CFR Part
107. This hampers the ability for prosecutors, corrections officials and law enforcement to effectively battle the rampant use of drones over correctional facilities.
In response to this lack of federal regulation, l3 states have passed various laws restricting the use of drones over or around prisons and other correctional facilities
(Arizona, Iowa, Louisiana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina,
Oregon, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah and Wisconsin).
LD 2157 would simply make it unlawful to either deliver or attempt to deliver
contraband to a prison using a drone or to operate a drone over of a correctional facility,
or to land a drone at the facility or to operate it from the facility. Exceptions are made in the bill, of course, for drones operated by corrections personnel and law enforcement
personnel using the drone lawfully in the performance of their duties.
LD 2157 is a common sense solution to a growing problem and I encourage the
committee to support it with a vote of `Ought To Pass' . I thank you for your time and will
gladly answer any questions to my ability.
Respectfully,

Senator Anne Beebe-Center, Chair Representative Tavis Hasenfus, Chair Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety 5 State House Station, Room 436 Augusta, ME 04333
RE: LD 2157: An Act to Prohibit the Unauthorized Use of Drones on or over the Premises of Correctional Facilities and Jails
Dear Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and Honorable Members of the Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety:
MACDL opposes LD 2157.
While we support reasonable measures that protect correctional institutions and staff, this proposal reaches far beyond its stated purpose and creates a broad new Class C felony that criminalizes innocent conduct, duplicates existing law, and invites arbitrary enforcement without meaningfully improving safety.
The bill targets the intentional conveyance of contraband by drone. However, it goes much further. It also makes it a felony simply to fly a drone over a correctional facility at or below 400 feet, land on the premises, or launch from the premises, regardless of purpose or intent. The State would not need to prove that the operator intended to deliver contraband, knew the location of the facility, or created any security risk.
The language risks criminalizing everyday, non-culpable behavior. A hobbyist, journalist, surveyor, contractor, or neighbor could inadvertently cross an invisible airspace boundary and commit a felony. Maine law traditionally ties felony liability to intentional or knowing misconduct. This bill departs from that principle.
The proposal also duplicates tools prosecutors already possess. Current law already prohibits conveying contraband into correctional facilities, and existing statutes cover attempt, conspiracy, and accomplice liability. If someone uses a drone to smuggle contraband, prosecutors can already charge that conduct. Creating a new felony that sweeps far beyond intentional smuggling adds little public-safety value while dramatically expanding criminal exposure.
We are particularly concerned that the bill imposes a Class C crime without a mens rea
1

requirement. In effect, it creates strict liability for conduct punishable by up to five years of incarceration and the lifelong consequences of a felony conviction. Maine rarely attaches such severe penalties to unintentional conduct. Proportionality and fairness require proof of intent or knowledge. For these reasons, the Maine Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers respectfully urges the Committee to reject L.D. 2157 Sincerely, /s/Jeremy Pratt Jeremy Pratt, Esq.

In Support of:
LD 2157, An Act to Prohibit the Unauthorized Use of Drones on or Over the Premises of Correctional Facilities
and Jails

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety
Committee, my name is Jill O'Brien, and I am the Director of Government Afiairs for the Maine Department of
Corrections.
I am testifying in support of LD 2157, An Act to Prohibit the Unauthorized Use of Drones on or Over the Premises of Correctional Facilities and Jails. This is a Department of Corrections bill that makes it a Class C crime to pilot a drone over the premises of a correctional facility Without permission fiom the chief admmistrative oflicer. The bill also clarifies that it is a Class C crime to use a drone to convey or attempt to convey prison contraband.
A bill prohibiting drones over correctional facilities is necessary to combat a growing nationwide problem of drones being
used to convey contraband like cell phones, drugs, and escape tools. Drones are also used to survey prison staff and security features to plan escapes.

In 2025, Georgia's Corrections Department detected nearly 400 drones attempting to bring contraband into its facilities. In
December of last year, a drone in South Carolina dropped marijuana, cigarettes, and food into a South Carolina prison. A
different drone in South Carolina dropped escape tools prior to that incident.

Contraband is not just a rules issue, it is a safety issue. Prison residents can use cell phones to contact victims and coordinate criminal activity. Substance use in Maine's prisons remains a danger to residents and staff, with a dozen residents and several staff last year requiring emergency room care after exposure to contraband substances. While Maine
does not know how those particular substances were brought into the prison, drones are frequently used to bring drugs
into prisons.

Presently, nothing prohibits flying a drone over a prison or jail in Maine, even though it is prohibited to fly one in Baxter
State Park. Park Rule 5.5 imposes a $1000 civil penalty for flying an unmanned aerial vehicle in the park.
New Hampshire passed a law outlawing the use of drones over correctional facilities that went into effect on January 1.
Tennessee and Arkansas have also recently passed similar laws.

This is a real problem facing not just other states but Maine too. Recently, multiple drones were detected over Long Creek and the Cumberland County Jail, and more than a dozen drones per day were detected over the Portland Intemational Jetport, very close to Long Creek.

Pass on LD 2157. I am happy to answer any questions. Thank you.'

RE: LD 2157

The Criminal Law Advisory Commission (CLAC)* respectfully submits the following testimony opposed to LD 2157 as currently drafted. CLAC's opposition stems from questions about the drafting approach, which we recognize may be addressed or resolved by the Department.
CLAC members noted that the conduct described in proposed � 761(1) ("use of a drone to convey or attempt to convey prison contraband in violation of section 757") could be charged under existing 17-A M.R.S. � 757. The proposal essentially creates a separate statute to criminalize a particular method of trafficking prison contraband.
Proposed � 761(1) does not include a culpable mental state. The manner in which it incorporates section 757 implies that the conduct must be committed "intentionally" (as in section 757). The culpable mental state element should be clarified.
Proposed � 761(2) is drafted as a strict liability crime ("...if a person in fact flies a drone..."). This drafting approach would subject a person to Class C prosecution for inadvertently flying a drone over a facility at or below 400 feet, and thus appears overly broad. CLAC members questioned whether there is a substantive difference in level of seriousness of the conduct between flying over a facility (recognizing that there is a security risk inherent in the ability of drones to record or photograph the premises, and that such conduct would not fall within existing section 757), and landing on or flying from the premises, but we did not have information regarding the reasons underlying the proposal.

Testimony of Patrick William Polky, Knox County Sheriff In Support of LD 2157: "An Act to Prohibit the Unauthorized Use of Drones on or
over the Premises of Correctional Facilities and Jails" Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
February 12, 2026

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Committee:

My name is Patrick Polky. I am the Sheriff of Knox County, and I am submitting this testimony in strong support of LD 2157. While I do not speak for the Maine Sheriffs' Association today, I know there is growing concern among my colleagues about the security gaps this issue presents to our county jails.

The Security Need In Knox County, we manage a correctional facility that is the backbone of our local public safety. As technology evolves, so do the methods used to bypass our security perimeters. We have seen nationally that unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are no longer just hobbyist toys; they are tools for conveying contraband--drugs, weapons, and cell phones--directly into the hands of the incarcerated, and for conducting surveillance and information gathering of security layouts and operations.

The rapid advancement of UAV technology has significantly increased these capabilities. Specifically, the rise of First-Person View (FPV) drones--which allow operators to navigate with extreme precision at high speeds--and the ability to override restricted airspace prompts pose unique and evolving threats to correctional operations. LD 2157 provides a necessary legal framework to deter and prosecute those who weaponize our airspace to undermine the safety and security of our correctional facilities. As you are aware, many of our incarcerated individuals participate in Medication Assisted Treatment (MAT), and the introduction of drugs outside of supervised care plans can prove fatal.

Critical Security Concerns for County Jails  Precision Contraband Delivery: Modern UAVs, particularly those used by organized criminal networks, can now carry payloads exceeding 20 pounds. FPV drones allow operators to fly through tight spaces or land directly at cell windows or within narrow recreation yards to deliver drugs, weapons, and electronic contraband like cell phones.

 Surveillance and Intelligence Gathering: Unauthorized drones are often used to monitor staff rotations, identify security vulnerabilities, or track inmate movements. This tactical intelligence can be used to coordinate escapes or plan assaults within the facility.
 Operational Interference: When an unidentified drone enters our airspace, it necessitates a facility lockdown. This disrupts essential services, including medical rounds, legal visits, and transports, while diverting limited law enforcement resources to attempt to locate the pilot.
 Limitations of Current Authority: Under federal law,drones are classified as "aircraft," which means local authorities are largely prohibited from physically intercepting them in flight. LD 2157 provides the necessary state-level enforcement mechanism to prosecute the operators on the ground.
Addressing the Technical Threat This bill correctly defines "drones" to include remotely piloted aircraft systems and micro air vehicles. For a county jail, even a "micro" drone can facilitate the delivery of high-potency narcotics, like fentanyl, which poses a lethal risk to our corrections officers and incarcerated individuals. By establishing a Class C crime for flying at or below 400 feet over our premises, this legislation gives my office the clear legal mandate to act when these devices are detected. Conclusion LD 2157 is a proactive and necessary step to modernize our criminal code for the 21st century. It ensures that the perimeters of the Knox County Jail and all of our correctional facilities extend vertically, protecting the integrity of our facilities and the safety of staff and the incarcerated in our care. I urge the Committee to vote "Ought to Pass" with the considerations mentioned above. Thank you for your time and for your commitment to the safety of Maine's citizens. Respectfully submitted,
Patrick W. Polky Sheriff, Knox County

My name is Sydney Bubar. I am a resident of Augusta and I oppose this bill as written.
"A person is guilty of unauthorized use of a drone on or over the premises of a correctional facility or jail if the person uses a drone to convey or attempt to convey prison contraband in violation of section 757." If the proposed bill ended here, that would make sense. It is indeed a violation of the law to deliver or receive contraband, no matter the delivery method.
However, later in the bill the insinuation is made that any and all "unauthorized use of a drone on or over the premises of a correctional facility or jail" would be a Class C crime.
The bill as proposed by Rep. Perkins of Dover-Foxcroft is disjointed and would set a dangerous precedent.
By prohibiting ALL drone usage over correctional facilities and jail via those properly licensed to use them, we would be restricting journalists, reporters, and human rights agencies from being able to obtain information regarding possible human rights violations.
Amid modern-day Jim Crow America and Nazi Germany, we must not allow needless oversight to restrict the people's constitutional ability to obtain information regarding the treatment of those currently in detention.
I urge those on this committee to vote Ought Not to Pass on the bill as it is currently written.
